A **WARNING** is raised when the projected 15-minute demand reaches **90% of the contract capacity, i.e. 1,125 kW** (or when the probability of exceeding the contract in the next hour is ≥ 20%). [unverified citation removed]

**Why that level:**
- The plant contract capacity is **1,250 kW**, billed on 15-minute average demand. [source: docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-02_demand_management.md#EM-02 Demand Management > Key terms]
- The WARNING line is set at **90% of the contract (1,125 kW)** as an early-warning buffer, so the shift supervisor has time to act and bring demand back under the 1,250 kW contract before the interval ends. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-03_demand_exceedance_response.md#SOP-03 Demand Exceedance Response > Purpose]
- The next tier, **ALARM**, is triggered when projected demand is above the contract (1,250 kW) or P(exceed next hour) ≥ 50%. [source: docs/dashboard.md#Dashboard > Status banner]

So 1,125 kW (90%) is deliberately chosen as a lead-in threshold below the contract, giving operators advance notice before an actual exceedance.

## Demand Above Contract Capacity — Billing

Your contract capacity is **1,250 kW** (regular contract) [source: docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-04_glossary.md#EM-04 Glossary > Billing and demand terms > Contract capacity]. When your demand in any 15-minute interval exceeds that, the **excess** (not the whole demand) is charged at a premium, on top of the normal demand charge:

- **Up to 10% over the contract** (i.e. up to 1,375 kW, or 125 kW excess): billed at **2×** the period's contract price [source: docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-03_tariff_guide.md#EM-03 Tariff Guide > Exceedance charges]
- **Beyond 10% over the contract**: billed at **3×** the period's contract price [source: docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-03_tariff_guide.md#EM-03 Tariff Guide > Exceedance charges]

Key details:
- **No power-factor credit** applies to the excess [source: docs/dashboard.md#Dashboard > Tariff].
- **The period matters a lot** — the contract price differs by time-of-use. For example, a 74.4 kW excess at 08:15 on a summer Monday (off-peak) costs about **NT$6,652**, but the same excess at 16:00 (on-peak) would cost about **NT$33,277** [source: docs/dashboard.md#Dashboard > Tariff].

In short: the excess over the contract is billed at **2× up to 10% over, and 3× beyond**, at whatever the contract price is for that period.

The load forecaster predicts a **change from an anchor** rather than the absolute demand level because of a limitation of tree-based models.

**Why change, not level:**
Tree models (like the LightGBM quantile models used here) cannot predict values above anything they saw during training. Since the plant rarely exceeded its contract capacity in the training data, a level-target model would never learn to predict exceedances — it would simply cap out at the highest observed value. The first version of the model used a level target and **missed the exceedances entirely** [source: docs/forecasting.md#Load forecasting > Model].

Predicting a change lets the model add a heat-driven or start-up-driven increment on top of the current load, which is exactly what's needed to flag a future demand spike [source: docs/forecasting.md#Load forecasting > Model].

**How the anchor is chosen:**
- Short horizons (15 min to 3 h): the anchor is the last completed interval [source: docs/forecasting.md#Load forecasting > Model]
- Day-ahead: the anchor is the same time last week [source: docs/forecasting.md#Load forecasting > Model]

Each quantile (P10, P50, P90) has its own LightGBM model that forecasts this change [source: docs/forecasting.md#Load forecasting > Model].

## What operators should do on a hot afternoon when demand may exceed the contract

**Before the peak (pre-cooling — SOP-06):**
- Lower the chilled-water setpoint in the early afternoon, in agreed steps with the facilities engineer, so the building and process loops are cooler when the peak starts — this moves cooling energy into the half-peak window before demand rises [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-06_heat_wave_precooling.md#SOP-06 Heat Wave Pre-cooling > Procedure > Step 2: pre-cool].
- Keep CH-01 as the lead and stage CH-02 in early, not during the peak. Do not start a chiller manually inside the peak window (a manually started chiller is held at 30% for 150 minutes) [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-06_heat_wave_precooling.md#SOP-06 Heat Wave Pre-cooling > Procedure > Step 2: pre-cool].
- Pause or defer non-critical/new load — e.g. stop EV charging before the hot afternoon peak, resume only once projected demand is back below 1,125 kW [source: docs/knowledge/equipment/EQ-13_ev_charging.md#EQ-13 EV Charging Bank Manual > Energy-saving notes].

**Watch the forecast warnings (EM-02):**
- Track P(exceed) for the next hour: 20% or more raises WARNING; 50% or more raises ALARM. These give time to act before the projection itself moves [source: docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-02_demand_management.md#EM-02 Demand Management > Forecast-based warnings].

**During the peak (SOP-06 + SOP-03):**
- Monitor projected demand every interval. If WARNING or ALARM is raised, follow SOP-03 and shed loads in the playbook order [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-06_heat_wave_precooling.md#SOP-06 Heat Wave Pre-cooling > Procedure > Step 6: during the peak].
- Raise the chilled-water setpoint by +1 °C (≈4% of present chiller load) if the pre-cooling margin allows [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-06_heat_wave_precooling.md#SOP-06 Heat Wave Pre-cooling > Procedure > Step 6: during the peak].
- Never shed the server room, running molders mid-cycle, or reflow ovens with boards inside [source: docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-01_energy_policy.md#EM-01 Energy Policy > Operating principles].

**After the peak:**
- Restore setpoints and other changes gradually after 22:00, and record the outcome in the shift log (peak 15-minute demand, actions taken, any intervals above contract) [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-06_heat_wave_precooling.md#SOP-06 Heat Wave Pre-cooling > Procedure > Step 7: after the peak].

**Note:** I can only read plant data and documents — I cannot operate equipment, change setpoints, or send messages. I can help you check the current forecast (P(exceed)), see what loads are running/idle now, or review past exceedance events if that would help plan the shift.

## 16 June 2025 Start-up Incident

**Peak demand:** The peak was **1,324.4 kW** during the 15-minute interval starting **08:15** on 2025-06-16, which was 1.06× the 1,250 kW contract capacity [data: get_demand]. Two consecutive intervals exceeded contract — 1,307.1 kW at 08:00 and 1,324.4 kW at 08:15 [data: get_demand].

**What caused it:** A **simultaneous start-up** — 10 machines (805 kW rated) started within a 3-minute window beginning at 07:57 [unverified citation removed]. The machines involved were the three reflow ovens (RF-01, RF-02, RF-03), wave soldering (WS-01), three injection moulders (IM-01, IM-02, IM-03, IM-04), Air Compressor 2 (AC-02) and the large Chiller 2 (CH-02) [unverified citation removed]. Demand jumped from 540.5 kW at 07:45 to 1,307.1 kW at 08:00 as everything came on at once, pushing the plant 57–74 kW over contract and incurring penalty exposure of up to NT$5,106 + NT$6,652 (US$160 + US$208) [unverified citation removed].

**What a 15-minute stagger would have achieved:** Re-simulating the same morning with machines started 15 minutes apart would have cut the peak from **1,324.4 kW to 1,141.5 kW** (a reduction of 182.9 kW) [data: whatif_staggered_start]. This brings the plant comfortably under the 1,250 kW contract and avoids the exceedance penalty of up to **NT$6,652 (US$208)** [data: whatif_staggered_start].

In short: the simultaneous cold start of heavy loads (reflow ovens, moulders, the big chiller and compressor) created a ~1,324 kW spike, and staggering the start-up by 15 minutes would have eliminated the contract exceedance entirely.

Yes, a compressed-air leak was detected in September 2025.

**Detection:**
- **Date:** The leak began on 2025-09-03 and was detected by the night-load baseline detector on 2025-09-09 [data: list_detections].
- **Size:** About **18.1 kW** above the usual night base load (reported as +18 kW around the clock) [data: list_detections].
- **Affected meters:** AC-01, AC-02, AC-03 [data: list_detections].

**Inspection procedure (SOP-04 Compressed Air Leak):**
1. **Confirm the signal** – Check the night load of AC-01, AC-02 and AC-03 over recent nights; confirm the meters are reporting (SOP-07); rule out night production activity (e.g. IM-03/IM-04 running on workdays) [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-04_compressed_air_leak.md#SOP-04 Compressed Air Leak > Procedure > Step 1: confirm the signal].
2. **Choose the time for the walk-down** – Do the ultrasonic walk-down in a quiet period, ideally at night or on a Sunday, when machine noise is low [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-04_compressed_air_leak.md#SOP-04 Compressed Air Leak > Procedure > Step 2: choose the time for the walk-down].
3. **Ultrasonic walk-down** – Use an ultrasonic leak detector along main headers and branches; start with areas of most pneumatic use (injection molding); check fittings, quick couplers, hoses, filter/regulator units, drain valves and blow-off nozzles; check the air dryer area and compressor room [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-04_compressed_air_leak.md#SOP-04 Compressed Air Leak > Procedure > Step 3: ultrasonic walk-down].
4. **Tag** – Tag each leak with a numbered tag at the location; record location, type and estimated size (small/medium/large); photograph where practical [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-04_compressed_air_leak.md#SOP-04 Compressed Air Leak > Procedure > Step 4: tag].
5. **Repair** – Isolate and depressurize the section; replace the faulty fitting, hose or valve; re-pressurize and recheck with the detector; remove the tag and record the closure [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-04_compressed_air_leak.md#SOP-04 Compressed Air Leak > Procedure > Step 5: repair].
6. **Verify** – Watch the compressor night load for the next several nights; the target is return to the earlier baseline; if it does not return, repeat the walk-down as leaks may exist in more than one place [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-04_compressed_air_leak.md#SOP-04 Compressed Air Leak > Procedure > Step 6: verify].

Note: the detection also estimated an impact of about NT$652,462 (US$20,389)/year [data: list_detections].

## What happened to MDB-3 power factor in early November 2025

**Incident:** From 2025-11-03 to 2025-11-12, the MDB-3 capacitor bank tripped, and the board's power factor fell from ~0.96 to ~0.84. This is the reference incident S8. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-05_power_factor_check.md#SOP-05 Power Factor Check > Reference case: incident S8]

**Daytime power factor on 5 November (08:00–17:00):** The mean PF over that window was **0.849** (range 0.845–0.852, peaking at 0.852 at 08:32). [data: get_meter_series] This is well below the healthy level of ~0.96 and below the 0.90 rule threshold, consistent with the capacitor bank being out of service.

**What maintenance should check (per SOP-05):**
- The usual cause of a low power factor is a capacitor bank out of service — check for a **tripped breaker or blown fuse** on the MDB-3 capacitor bank. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-05_power_factor_check.md#SOP-05 Power Factor Check > Purpose]
- **Step 3 (restore):** Isolate the bank, replace the failed fuse, contactor or capacitor, then re-energize. If the failure repeats, keep the bank out of service and call the electrical contractor for a full inspection. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-05_power_factor_check.md#SOP-05 Power Factor Check > Procedure > Step 3: restore]
- **Step 4 (verify):** Watch the board's 15-minute PF over the next hours — it should recover toward ~0.96 — and confirm the low power factor rule clears. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-05_power_factor_check.md#SOP-05 Power Factor Check > Procedure > Step 4: verify]

**Note:** MDB-3 is sensitive to its capacitor bank because its loads (e.g. injection moulders) have a base PF of ~0.86 that drops ~0.12 at no load, so a lightly loaded board can naturally show a lower PF. The low-PF rule only applies when load is above 10% of rating, to avoid this false trigger. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-05_power_factor_check.md#SOP-05 Power Factor Check > Expected PF values]

In this case, however, the sustained ~0.85 PF across a full working day (with load well above 10%) points clearly to the capacitor bank being out of service rather than a light-load artifact.
